δόξα ἀναπέμπεται. 19.26 πάλιν τοῦ Μάρκου λέγοντος ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ· «ὃς γὰρ ἂν ἐπαισχυνθῇ με καὶ τοὺς ἐμοὺς λόγους ἐν τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ τῇ μοι χαλίδι καὶ ἁμαρτωλῷ, καὶ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐπαισχυνθήσεται αὐτόν, ὅταν ἔλθῃ ἐν τῇ δόξῃ τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ μετὰ τῶν ἀγγέλων τῶν ἁγίων». 19.27 Ὁ Ματθαῖος τὸ αὐτὸ κεφάλαιον ἐκτιθέμενος οὐκ εἶπεν· «ἐν τῇ τοῦ πατρός», ἀλλ' «ἐν τῇ τοῦ υἱοῦ», οὕτω γράψας· «ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐν τῇ δόξῃ αὐτοῦ 23 καὶ πάντες οἱ ἅγιοι ἄγγελοι μετ' αὐτοῦ, ὅτε καθίσῃ ἐπὶ θρόνου δόξης αὐτοῦ». καὶ παρ' Ἰωάννῃ δέ φησιν· «δόξασόν με τῇ δόξῃ, ᾗ εἶχον παρὰ σοὶ πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι». 20.ν Περὶ τοῦ διὰ τὸ ὁμοούσιον καὶ ἰσοδύναμον κατοικεῖν ἐν πιστοῖς τόν τε πατέρα τόν τε υἱὸν τό τε ἅγιον πνεῦμα· καὶ πρὸς τὴν τῶν ἑτεροδόξων ἀντίθεσιν. 20.1 Εὑρήσομεν ἔτι τὸ ὁμοούσιον And in John also he says: 'glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world was.' 20.ν [Chapter title:] About the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit dwelling in believers on account of the sameness of substance and equal power; and toward the opposition of those of other opinion. 20.1 We will find further the sameness of substance of the Trinity and how without variation all things are possible to it, if we perceive that it alone, being above the immaterial and invisible, can be partaken of according to substance and fill the temple which it created. 20.2 And to it not only this matter but also the word fits. 20.3 For on the partakable follows the unchangeable, and on this the uncreated, which is also the beginningless. 20.4 But nothing created, as far as from the custom of the Scriptures, can be partaken of in the manner of participation or fill the human being substantially, but only by the things of the good or the bad habit. 20.5 For metaphorically we say that some have been filled with virtue and knowledge and are able, in a contemplated way, to bring forth the rewards of virtue and knowledge, as those who have unmixedly received a share of the grace of the Holy Spirit. 20.6 It is attested then that both the Father and the Son and the Spirit dwell in us; as when Paul writes to Corinthians the second time from Jeremiah: 'for we are a temple of the living God, just as God said: I will dwell in them and walk about among them and will be their God and they will be my people.' pass_b_english: … “And I will not give my glory to another” (Isaiah 42:8); while John says, “that all may honour the Son just as they honour the Father” (John 5:23). For he already knew clearly that the glory is not offered up to the Only-begotten and to the Holy Spirit as to beings of another substance.

Again, Mark says, from Christ’s own lips: “For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him the Son of Man will also be ashamed, when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels” (Mark 8:38). Matthew, setting out the same passage, did not say “in the glory of the Father” but “in the glory of the Son,” writing thus: “But when the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, when he sits on the throne of his glory” (Matthew 25:31). And in John too he says: “Glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world was” (John 17:5).
That the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit dwell in the faithful because they are of one substance and equal in power; and a reply to the objection of those who think otherwise.

We shall find the oneness of substance of the Trinity, and that all things are possible to it without any difference, in yet another way, if we see that it alone, being beyond even what is immaterial and invisible, can be shared in according to substance, and can fill the temple it has created. And not only does the thing itself belong to it, but the word fits it as well. For being shared in brings with it being unchangeable, and that in turn being uncreated, which is also being without beginning.

But nothing created, as far as the usage of the Scriptures goes, can be shared in by way of participation, or fill a human being in substance; it can do so only in the way that a good or a bad disposition does. For it is by a figure of speech that we say some people are filled with virtue and knowledge, and are able, with understanding, to bring forth the rewards of virtue and knowledge, like those who have received an unmixed share in the grace of the Holy Spirit.

It is attested, then, that the Father, the Son and the Spirit dwell in us; as when Paul, writing to the Corinthians the second time, says from Jeremiah: “For we are the temple of the living God; as God said: I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (2 Corinthians 6:16). choices.issue: Workroom title, dropped paragraphs, garbled clauses
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old row was titled 'Unit 6 rem mid'; it printed the edition chapter number ('20.') before the chapter title and ran the title into the text; it broke off at 'For we speak metaphorically […]', dropping the rest of 20.5 and all of 20.6 (the indwelling of Father, Son and Spirit proved from 2 Corinthians 6:16 and 1 Corinthians 3:16); it rendered ἀπαραλλάκτως 'unchangeably' (it is 'without difference', between the Persons) and made 20.4 end 'only matters of a good or a bad disposition' without saying what they do. References: '(Isa 42:8)' and '(Matt 25:31)' written in full; 2 Corinthians 6:16 and 1 Corinthians 3:16 added.

choices.why: The section opens with the quotation that the previous section's last words ('who has said in Isaiah:') introduce; the μέν … δέ balance is kept with 'while'. Leading ellipsis marks the sentence begun earlier.
The subject is not named; it can be God speaking in Isaiah or John. English keeps the unnamed 'he'.

choices.english: the glory is not offered up to the Only-begotten and to the Holy Spirit as to beings of another substance
choices.why: ἀναπέμπω is the word for offering up praise; the point is that glory given to Son and Spirit is not glory given 'to another'.

choices.english: That the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit dwell in the faithful … and a reply to the objection of those who think otherwise.
choices.why: Chapter title made its own short paragraph without the edition number; ἑτερόδοξοι rendered 'those who think otherwise'.

choices.english: being beyond even what is immaterial and invisible
choices.why: Didymus places the Trinity above immaterial created beings too; 'even' marks that sense.

choices.term: οὐ τὸ πρᾶγμα τοῦτο μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ λέξις ἁρμόζει
choices.english: not only does the thing itself belong to it, but the word fits it as well
choices.why: The reality (being shared in, filling) and the vocabulary for it both properly apply to the Trinity alone.

choices.why: The dative is compressed; 20.5 explains it (we say people are 'filled' with virtue only by a figure). English supplies the verb the Greek leaves understood; no bracket, as the sense is not in doubt.
